snip.t: *Splenomegaly:* Reticuloendothelial hyperplasia responding to cleared red cells or intracellular pathogens (malaria, visceral leishmaniasis/kala-azar, brucellosis, schistosomiasis, typhoid).
| Visceral leishmaniasis | Months of fever, massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia | Bone marrow or splenic aspirate shows LD bodies |
Can indicate disseminated fungal infections (e.g., Cryptococcosis, Histoplasmosis, Sporotrichosis), cutaneous leishmaniasis, or larval migrans.
Rashes, papules, nodules, ulcers: Direct manifestation of infection (e.g., Cryptococcal skin lesions, Kaposi's sarcoma in HIV, cutaneous leishmaniasis).

qs.q: Which Leishmania species complex causes anthroponotic visceral leishmaniasis?
o: Leishmania donovani causing anthroponotic visceral leishmaniasis
Leishmania infantum causing anthroponotic visceral leishmaniasis
Leishmania major causing anthroponotic visceral leishmaniasis
Leishmania tropica causing anthroponotic visceral leishmaniasis
qs.e: Visceral leishmaniasis is caused by the Leishmania donovani complex, specifically with L. donovani responsible for anthroponotic transmission and L. infantum responsible for zoonotic transmission. Other species like L. major cause cutaneous forms.

qs.q: What is the gold standard diagnostic procedure for confirming visceral leishmaniasis?
o: Demonstration of amastigotes in tissue aspirate smears
Indirect immunofluorescent antibody test performed in serum
Leishmanin skin test performed using intradermal injection
Polymerase chain reaction applied on peripheral blood
qs.e: Demonstration of amastigotes in Giemsa-stained smears of tissue aspirates is the gold standard for diagnosing visceral leishmaniasis. Splenic smears have a particularly high sensitivity exceeding 95%.

qs.q: Which tissue aspirate site yields the highest sensitivity (>95%) for demonstrating amastigotes in visceral leishmaniasis?
o: Spleen yielding highest sensitivity for amastigotes
Bone marrow yielding highest sensitivity for amastigotes
Lymph node yielding highest sensitivity for amastigotes
Liver yielding highest sensitivity for amastigotes
qs.e: Splenic smears have a sensitivity of greater than 95%, making it the highest yield tissue aspirate site compared to bone marrow (60–85%) and lymph nodes (50%).

qs.q: What is the traditional first-line drug class used for visceral leishmaniasis in most endemic regions, despite rising resistance in some areas?
o: Pentavalent antimonials used for visceral leishmaniasis
Macrolide antibiotics used for visceral leishmaniasis
First-generation cephalosporins used for visceral leishmaniasis
Nucleoside analogues used for visceral leishmaniasis
qs.e: Pentavalent antimonials (such as sodium stibogluconate and meglumine antimoniate) are the drug of choice for visceral leishmaniasis in most endemic regions, though resistance occurs in areas like Bihar, India.

qs.q: Which of the following is the first oral compound approved for the treatment of leishmaniasis?
o: Miltefosine approved as the first oral compound
Paromomycin approved as the first oral compound
Fluconazole approved as the first oral compound
Chloroquine approved as the first oral compound
qs.e: Miltefosine is the first oral compound approved for the treatment of leishmaniasis. Because of its long half-life, it is prone to inducing drug resistance.

qs.q: Which specific drug of choice is recommended for treating HIV and visceral leishmaniasis co-infections?
o: Liposomal Amphotericin B for coinfection treatment
Sodium stibogluconate for coinfection treatment
Oral Miltefosine monotherapy for coinfection treatment
Pentamidine alone utilized for coinfection treatment
qs.e: Liposomal Amphotericin B is the drug of choice for HIV and visceral leishmaniasis co-infection, where VL behaves as an opportunistic infection and serodiagnostic tests are commonly negative.

qs.q: What is a common clinical feature observed in East African patients who develop Post Kala-azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL)?
o: Majority of patients experience spontaneous healing
Universal requirement for prolonged intravenous amphotericin B
Rapid progression to visceral organ failure within weeks
Exclusive involvement of the central nervous system
qs.e: In East Africa, a majority of patients with Post Kala-azar Dermal Leishmaniasis experience spontaneous healing, unlike Indian cases which are typically treated with pentavalent antimonials for 60–120 days.

qs.q: Following successful treatment for visceral leishmaniasis, which clinical sign typically improves first within the first week?
o: Defervescence and symptom improvement first
Complete regression of splenomegaly first
Normalization of skin pigmentation first
Total clearance of hepatomegaly first
qs.e: Within a week after the start of treatment, defervescence, weight gain, and recovery of hematologic parameters are evident, whereas complete regression of splenomegaly takes months.

es.q: Outline environmental and personal measures used to control leishmaniasis transmission.
es.m:
- Reduce contact between people and infected sandflies.
- Use insecticide-treated or fine-mesh bed nets and appropriate repellents where indicated.
- Improve housing to reduce sandfly entry and resting sites.
- Apply targeted vector-control measures such as residual insecticide spraying when appropriate.
- Diagnose and treat human cases and address relevant animal reservoirs according to the local transmission cycle.

ai.summary: Leishmaniasis is a parasitic disease transmitted by sandflies, presenting as cutaneous, mucocutaneous, or visceral forms. Diagnosis relies on clinical clues and parasite detection; treatment targets the parasite while managing complications.

sections.p: Leishmaniasis is caused by Leishmania spp., transmitted by sandfly bites. Visceral disease (kala-azar) shows fever, weight loss, splenomegaly; cutaneous lesions are ulcerative. Diagnosis requires parasite identification (skin smear, splenic aspirate) or serology (rK39).

t.b: Detects antibodies; positive suggests visceral leishmaniasis, but false‑negative in early disease.
Confirms amastigotes; high sensitivity but invasive.
Detects parasite DNA; useful when microscopy is negative.

sections.p: Visceral leishmaniasis is staged by clinical severity: mild (fever, mild splenomegaly), moderate (anemia, thrombocytopenia), severe (splenic rupture, septicemia). Cutaneous disease is staged by ulcer size and number.
Primary cause is sandfly bite in endemic areas. Co‑factors include HIV, malnutrition, and chronic infections such as tuberculosis or malaria, which worsen outcomes.

Visceral leishmaniasis presents with prolonged fever, weight loss, pallor, splenomegaly, and pancytopenia. Cutaneous forms start as papules that ulcerate; mucocutaneous disease involves nasal or oral mucosa.
Key tests confirm parasite presence and assess severity. When resources are limited, a simple smear and CBC can guide management.

Screening tool; positive supports diagnosis when microscopy unavailable.

sections.p: Urgent complications include splenic rupture, severe anemia, septicemia, and post‑kala‑azar dermal leishmaniasis. Red flags: sudden abdominal pain, bleeding, altered consciousness.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden abdominal pain (splenic rupture), severe bleeding, confusion, or any sign of septic shock

faq.q: Can leishmaniasis be transmitted by blood transfusion?
faq.a: Yes, especially visceral leishmaniasis; screening of donors in endemic areas is advised.

faq.q: Is there a vaccine for leishmaniasis?
faq.a: No licensed vaccine exists; prevention relies on vector control and early treatment.
Yes, relapse and post‑kala‑azar dermal leishmaniasis can occur, especially in HIV‑infected patients.
